noticias.antetitulo: AI and age in the classroom
noticias.titular: The age for using AI in class depends on three different rules: those of the companies, the law and the education authorities
noticias.entradilla: Each service’s terms, data protection law and some education authorities set different ages for using artificial intelligence, and they are often confused. This report explains what each says as of 6 November 2026, why research asks us to swap the question of age for the question of purpose, and how a primary or secondary teacher can decide which tool to use, with which account, and who operates it.
noticias.imagen_alt: Infographic on an age ruler from 0 to 18, with marks at 13, 14 and 18, in three blocks. “Companies”: “OpenAI and Microsoft: from 13”, with a line from 13 to 18; “Anthropic: from 18”, with a dot at 18; and “Gemini with a school account: all ages”, with a bar from 0 to 18. “Data law”: “Own consent: from 14”, with a dashed line up to 14 and a solid one after it; and “At school, no consent needed: educational function”, with a bar from 0 to 18. “Some education authorities”: “Catalonia: the teacher operates the AI”, with a red line up to 14, and “From 14: inform, authorisation advisable”, with a line from 14; and “Basque Country: chatbots from 13”, with a cross before 13 and a line after it; and “Murcia: autonomous access from Year 3 of ESO”, with a dashed line up to 14 and a solid one after it. At the foot, “What for? Which account? Who operates it?”.

noticias.titular: Handing tasks to an AI agent means deciding first what it can see, remember and do
noticias.entradilla: Artificial intelligence assistants no longer just answer questions: they open folders, read email and act on behalf of the people who use them. Spain’s data protection authority has just published a ten-point guide to delegating without losing control. This report explains what changes, what companies and administrations say, and what a teacher can configure before granting an agent any permissions.
noticias.imagen_alt: Three overlapping circles, “Reads others’ content”, “Sensitive data” and “Acts alone”; in the overlaps of two, the safeguards “Read-only”, “No names” and “Ask for confirmation”, and in the centre, where all three meet, a red cross marked “Unacceptable risk”; at the bottom, a strip of five icons (eye, notebook, cursor, envelope and two people) for the AEPD’s five questions before delegating.
